en: The eighth chapter states the qualities (guṇas):
Just as the attributes such as valor belong to that which has attained the status of the primary element (aṅgin), [so do the qualities belong to the rasa].
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) He begins the examination of the qualities by saying "he states the qualities. Regarding the phrase "the state of being the principal for one who has attained [perfection]":

And this [statement] that "the poem is the subordinate member (aṅga) and rasa is the principal member (aṅgin)" is intended solely to demonstrate this very point; it does not, however, exclude rasa from being a subordinate member, because sweetness (mādhurya) and other qualities are experienced even there. Furthermore, the term *rasa* refers to that in which the sequence [of cognition] is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), since qualities (*guṇa*) are admitted even in the case of transitory emotions (*bhāva*) and the like. — *Locanā*.
(Lo, a) Having thus examined the defects, he introduces the examination of the excellences:
"The status of being the primary element belongs to the *rasa* because it constitutes the very soul of poetry;
the excellences—"
Just as qualities such as valor are designated by the term "guṇa" because they serve as causes for the excellence of a person who has attained the status of being the principal subject (*aṅgin*),

so too the properties of rasa— which has attained the status of being the principal subject in poetry— namely its specific characteristics such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and the rest, also possess the suitability that makes the composition of words conveying them fit to be designated as "poetry.
This is the meaning.
And how these [qualities] possess the nature of being mere taste has already been demonstrated.

In the *Vijñapriyā* (vi, kha), by the phrase "of that which has attained the state of being a constituent," the embodied self (*śarīrin*) is brought to mind; therefore, he provides an illustration with the words "just as indeed... and so forth.

"Specificities of their own nature" means specificities that distinguish them by way of their distinct characteristics (*vailakṣaṇya*), serving to differentiate them from others. "That which presents its own [quality]" refers to the collection of words that conveys or makes known its own quality; the suitability of that collection for the designation "poetry" consists in its conformity with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) residing within it in the poem.
The meaning is that they possess that form of stability.
Since that which is devoid of aesthetic flavor (nīrasa) cannot be denoted by the word "poetry" (kāvya), the term "poetry" is used there only in a figurative sense (lākṣaṇika).

Although qualities (guṇas) are manifested by phonemes (varṇas) alone and not by words, such that a collection of words lacks the capacity to impart those qualities, nevertheless, because they are imparted by the phonemes that constitute the collection of words, [the collection is so designated].
It is logical that even a collection of words possesses the capacity to convey that [rasa]. By demonstrating its compatibility, the category of *guṇa* (excellence) has been explained;
thus, it has been shown that these are properties belonging exclusively to rasa.
The meaning is that it is shown by the example of heroism (*śaurya*). By the word "only" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of its being a property of color (*varṇadharma*). — *Locanā* —
After the words "yathā khalu," the word "loke" (in the world) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

That collection of words which conveys sweetness and so forth of its own self—that is, which implants them within the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*)—is what is meant by "conformity thereto" (*tadanuguṇatvam*).
Although sweetness and the other qualities do not serve as causes for excellence because they constitute the very essence of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), [they are nevertheless considered so].

Nevertheless, because the capacity for such suggestion (vyañjakatva) in a composition of words depends solely on looking toward that [suggestion], and because the composition is fashioned according to the rules stated in such passages as "the stops (sparśa) ending in the last letter of each class [of consonants] reside at the head [of their respective groups]," it has its cause therein.

Thus, it was demonstrated in the first chapter that the quality of sweetness (mādhurya) and so forth— which consists in the excellence of rasa— is metaphorically attributed to the composition of words due to its conformity with that [suggestion].
Sweetness, vigor, and clarity—these are the three [qualities].
Locanā: (lo,
i) Because each of the three types mentioned by the ancients will be refuted as being of ten kinds,
those are the qualities.
In that regard—
the aesthetic delight (*ānanda*) consisting of the melting of the mind is called sweetness (*mādhurya*).
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ga) He states the definition of sweetness (*mādhuryya*): "The melting of the mind" (*cittadravī*). Here, the suffix *-mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). In the word *āhlāda*, it functions as a specific kind of delight. That specific delight—which arises from the bliss born of the knowledge of love (*rati*) and so forth, is apprehended by the operation called "savoring" (*svādana*), and constitutes the very nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—is what possesses sweetness; however, sweetness is not merely that specific delight itself, for in that case, it would be impossible for it to be a property of *rasa*. Thus, the meaning is: sweetness is the property that delimits such delight, which is the function of the delight whose nature is the melting of the mind.
Locanā:
(Lo, ī) "Bliss" (*hlāda*) means that whose nature is bliss; for its distinctness from that [ordinary pleasure] has been stated.

And here, since "taste" (*āsvāda*) is a synonym for "bliss" (*ānanda*), it is unique to aesthetic relish (*svāda*); thus, by the phrase "consisting of the melting of the mind," the charge of being too narrow (*avyāpti*) is avoided.
As for what has been stated by someone—that "sweetness (*mādhurya*) is the cause of melting (*druti*)"—that is not correct;
for since the state of melting is non-different from the bliss that constitutes the very nature of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), it cannot be its effect.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, gha) He says "As for that which... in order to refute what was stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
"Sweetness (*mādhurya*) is the quality of being delightful; its definition is that it is the cause of melting (*druti*) in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

This means that it is a property residing in [the emotion of] love (*rati*) and so forth, which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the production of the delight that constitutes the very nature of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Since passion (*rati*) and the like attain the state of being aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), they too possess the nature of *rasa*;
the meaning is that this very quality is the cause of the melting (*druti*) of the mind.
He refutes this, saying: "That is not so."
Regarding the phrase "of the state of liquefaction" (*dravībhāvasya*): it refers to the state of not producing its own substratum and so forth by itself.
This has been refuted by [the author] himself after first accepting the non-difference between liquefaction and bliss (*āhlāda*).

However, in that [opponent's] view, liquefaction is a modification of the mind (*cittavṛtti*) while bliss is a modification of the self (*ātmavṛtti*); thus, there is no non-difference between these two at all.

However, it is precisely through the sweetness of passion (*rāga-mādhurya*) that the melting of the heart (*citta-dravībhāva*) is produced by means of a sweetness residing in aesthetic delight (*āhlāda*). Furthermore, this "melting" consists in the state of the connoisseur’s heart becoming predominantly moist (*ārdraprāyatva*), brought about by the arousal of bliss permeated by the form of love (*rati*) and other such sentiments; this occurs through the abandonment of natural stiffness (*svābhāvika-anāviṣṭatva-ātmaka-kāṭhinya*), as well as the agitation caused by pride, anger, and so forth, and the distraction induced by brilliance, wrath, wonder, laughter, and the like. (Vijñapriyā)

(vi, ṅa) He demonstrates the state of melting (*dravībhāva*), which has been described as being non-different from the joy consisting of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), with the words "and the state of melting.
For the very state of being permeated by the mind is indeed the state of melting.

Its unpermeated state, however, is its natural condition; and the two—resentment and anger, which take the form of the zeal to kill an enemy—are produced by that inherent hardness (*kāṭhinya*) which constitutes its nature.

Taking that as the starting point, there is the agitation and restlessness of the mind caused by heat, physical glow, radiance, wonder, and laughter, and so forth; by abandoning those, there arises—by virtue of the mind being permeated—a bliss consisting of knowledge whose form is suffused with *rati* (erotic passion) and other such states, having as its object the very essence of *rati* and the like.
Through the awakening of that [bliss], the state of being "moist" (*ārdraprāyatva*)—that is, the melting (*dravībhāva*)—of the heart of the connoisseur (*sahr̥daya*) occurs. This is the meaning.
It should be noted that this established doctrine is possible only if joy (*āhlāda*) is accepted as being a mental modification (*manovṛtti*);
otherwise, the statement regarding the non-difference between melting (*druti*) and joy would be untenable.

In the phrase "having the form of love and so forth" (*ratyādyākāra*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the permanent moods (*sthāyibhāva*) of the pathetic (*karuṇa*) and peaceful (*śānta*) sentiments, which are the substrata of sweetness (*mādhurya*).
Thus, *rasa* is precisely that specific exhilaration (*āhlāda*) produced by the bliss of knowledge regarding love and other such [emotions].

It has been stated previously that this very [exhilaration] is what is reached through the operation called "tasting" (*svādana*), and it is established as the doctrine that sweetness (*mādhurya*) is a specific attribute residing within that [exhilaration].
Locanā:
Regarding "intrinsic" (*svābhāvika*)—the intrinsic is the innate state of non-penetration (*anāviṣṭatva*), which, by implication, is the very nature of the mind itself as solidity;
likewise, it is that brilliance produced by passion, anger, and so forth, as in the case of a hero and the like.
Thus, by the abandonment—that is, the avoidance—of that distraction which is accompanied by wonder and laughter, as in the case of the marvelous (*adbhuta*) and so forth;
this is of the quality called *mādhurya* (sweetness).
And that—
He is compassionate toward those experiencing union, more so toward those experiencing separation, and most of all toward those who are peaceful; thus, in sequence.
Vijñapriyā:
"And that" means "and that sweetness.
Its gradual increase occurs because, in the stages beginning with *sambhoga*, there is a progressive intensification of the melting of the mind (*cittadruti*).
Locanā:
(lo, ū) "In the peaceful [state], it is more" means that because of its beauty consisting of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), it possesses sweetness as a general rule; thus, it is indeed preeminent.
In some cases, however, there is a distinction when accompanied by revulsion toward sense objects and so forth.
Terms such as "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*) and the like are mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*);
therefore, its persistence should be understood to exist even in the semblances of enjoyment and so on.

Excluding the eight letters ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, and ḍha, the letters joined with the final letter of their respective groups at the head [of each class], along with ra and ṇa, are the light [vowels]; these letters have become the causes for the manifestation of that [sound]. (VisSd 8.3)
The composition is sweet, characterized by the absence of repetition or only minimal repetition.
Vijñapriyā (vi, cha) states the following regarding the phonemes that manifest this quality: "In the head... and so forth.
The grammatical connection is that [the vowels] are joined with the fifth letter of their respective classes. In that very context, it excludes *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *ḍha*;
however, the letter *ta* is not excluded when placed above them.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the absence of *samdhi*] serves as the cause for manifesting sweetness (*mādhurya*) in its specific expression.
"Absence of repetition" (*avṛtti*) means the absence of compound (*asamāsa*).

As for "structure" (*racanā*), it refers to euphonic combination (*sandhi*); and although such [euphonic] letters would naturally result in the quality of sweet-sounding letters by virtue of the sweetness inherent in the letters produced by them, the purpose of the poet's instruction is to show that even in the case of *sandhi*, such letters are not those [specifically] resulting from *ūha* and so forth.
It is stated separately.
Locanā:

(lo, ṛ) "On the crown" means that the five groups beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, having become five groups of five, their final letters are *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*; joined with those situated on the crown, it follows that they belong to their own respective groups.
Likewise,
the letters ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, and ḍha— neither joined with a final consonant nor standing in their own form— are [heavy]; however,
*ra* and *ṇa* are light when separated by a short vowel.
In the manifestation of that sweetness (*mādhurya*), thus there are those without compounds and those with few compounds;
when joined with other words, they are sweet and possess sweetness.
For example:
"The flickering glances of her, the auspicious ground for the god of love,
repeatedly produce a continuous stream of internal torment within young men."
Vijñapriyā:

In the example beginning with "aneṅga," there are two such syllables produced by sandhi; in the phrase "santāpasantati," there are likewise only two [syllables] resulting from the sandhi of the prefix and the verbal root.
Or as it is in my own verse:
“Causing the cluster of bees, intoxicated with nectar, to hum in the vine-thicket; swiftly inflaming the bodiless god of love as he embraces his own limbs;
gently stirring the blossomed lotus; and gathering the mass of pollen—it scatters nectar in every direction.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) Therefore, in order to show many such descriptive epithets (*varṇa*), he says "or as follows" (*yathā vā*).
The wind scatters nectar (*makaranda*) in every direction.
Of what kind?
Slowly and gently causing to tremble a bower of creepers where there was a swarm of bees intoxicated with honey;
[and] embracing, that is to say, the bodies of men.
And by rapidly increasing the bodiless god [Kāma], making him preeminent and powerful;
and by causing the lotus—already burst open and expanded—to tremble;
he obtains (*vindan*), that is, receives, a mass of pollen (*rajovṛnda*) from the blossomed lotuses (from the root *vidl*, "to obtain").
In this regard, even in the case of euphonic combinations (*saṃdhi*), many phonemes (*varṇa*) of the aforementioned forms occur.
Locanā:
In examples such as *latākuñjam*, even when there is merely a description of the setting, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) arises by virtue of the context.
Ojas is said to be the radiance of the mind, which takes the form of its expansion.
However, this [quality] reaches its highest degree respectively in the heroic (*vīra*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and the furious (*raudra*) sentiments.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ña): He states the definition of *ojas* as "of the mind... and so forth.
Here too, the meaning is simply "that which produces radiance," just as in the expression "clarified butter [is] life.
Thus, the meaning is that the radiance of the mind, in the form of expansion, is produced by the *ojas* residing in the *rasa*.
On this very point, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* has also stated that *ojas* (vigor) is that which produces expansion and brilliance of the mind.
Expansion, however, is a specific conjunction with the self (*ātman*) that causes the mind to become predominantly heated;
for otherwise, according to the literal sense, it would be untenable for the brilliance of the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) to reside in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
"Increasing order" means that there is an increase due to the increase in the result, which is the nature of brilliance;
this refers to *ojas*.
Here too, words such as "heroic" (*vīra*) and so forth are merely illustrative.
Therefore, its presence is also established in cases such as the semblance of a hero (*vīrābhāsa*).
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) And here, although not explicitly stated, it follows by virtue of propriety alone.
In the comic (*hāsya*), because its nature is expansion, and because *ojas* generally resides in the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), there is a preeminence of *mādhurya*.

In the terrifying (*bhayānaka*), although there is *mādhurya* due to the absence of expansion in the mental state (*cittavṛtti*), nevertheless, there is an infusion of *ojas* due to the appropriateness of the excitants (*vibhāva*).
In the marvelous (*adbhuta*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), there is a balance between the two;
here, *ojas* (vigorous energy) is predominant.
Although *ojas* is most intense in the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), nevertheless, *mādhurya* (sweetness) is not less so.
When the first and third letters of a group are absent, those at the end of the group are joined together.
Above or below, or in both positions, the letter *ra* together with *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *ḍha*, as well as *śa* and *ṣa*, have become its manifestors. (VisSd 8.6)
Likewise, there is an abundance of compounds, characterized by a boldness of composition.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ)—the meaning is this: from *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* [arise] *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *tha*, and *pha*.
The letters *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, and *bha* are joined with *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, *da*, and *ba*.
For example: “*cañcadbhuja-*,” and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭa) He states their manifestors: "of the class" (*vargasya*) and so forth. Regarding "the last two":
this means that for the first and third [classes], the last two are the second and fourth [consonants].
Thus, the second [consonant] is joined with the first;
the fourth letter is joined with the third—this is the meaning.
There is no rule that the first and third, or the last two, must belong to the same class (*varga*).

However, it should be understood that this same principle applies even to those belonging to different groups. Therefore, just as *ka-kha* and *ga-gha* are paired, so too should *ke-ccha* and *ge-ccha* be understood as such, due to their common pungency (*kaṭutva*).

Furthermore, although not explicitly stated here, the "union of similar sounds" (*tulyayoga*) mentioned by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* should also be accepted, as there is no difference in their pungency.
By this, forms such as *kka* and *gga* should also be understood; likewise,
in cases such as *upary-adhaḥ* and *tarka*, [the suffix] *upari* [is applied].
In examples such as *takracakra* and *adhaḥ-ārdraka*, two *repha*s (the letter *r*) are to be understood;

this is because of the phrase "together with *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, and *ḍha*. This "togetherness" (*sāhitya*) is mentioned by way of explaining their manifesting power (*vyañjakatva*), since they manifest [the sound] even when the consonants are joined with one another.
Regarding the phrase "composition (*ghaṭanā*) abounding in compounds," the word *ghaṭanā* refers both to mere arrangement and to euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
Therefore, the meaning is: an arrangement characterized by an abundance of compounds—that is, long compounds—and a euphonic combination endowed with boldness and pungency.
The passage beginning with *cañcaddbhuja* has been explained in the section on drama (*nāṭya*).
Here, there is a long compound consisting of a few syllables as previously described.
That which quickly pervades the mind is like fire in dry fuel. (VisSd 8.7)
That clarity (*prasāda*) exists in all sentiments (*rasas*) and compositions.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭha): He states the definition of the quality of clarity (*prasādaguṇa*)—beginning with "the mind" (*cittam*).
In this context, the term *citta* refers to *jñāna* (knowledge).
Thus, it is that quality which quickly pervades, reveals, or—so to speak—produces the understanding of the meaning of the verse;
for this very reason, he will later explain it as "it reveals."
That quality is *prasāda* (transparency/clarity); this is the meaning. Here he provides an illustration with the words "dry" and so forth:
just as fire quickly and most excellently manifests dry fuel—this is the meaning.
"In all the aesthetic sentiments" (samasteṣu raseṣu) and "in compositions" (racanāsu): here,
the locative case denotes the sense of location (adhikaraṇatā).
"Composition" (*racanā*) means the arrangement of words; here, it refers to the seventh [quality], namely suggestiveness (*vyañjakatā*).
Thus, the meaning is that all compositions are suggested by it.
Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be no non-sublime (*aloka*) work devoid of clarity (*prasāda*).
The meaning is: "in all types of compositions, but not in every individual instance of a composition."—
Locanā.

The meaning is that [the word] pervades the minds of those who practice it; it manifests [the object]. Sounds are the manifestors of that [word], which bring about the cognition of the object through mere hearing. (VisSd 8.8)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍa) He shows the manifestation of the composition that suggests that [meaning]: "words" (*śabdāḥ*). The meaning is that words which convey the object through mere hearing are the suggestors (*vyañjakāḥ*) of that [meaning].
Locanā:

(lo, ai) And here, because the quality of clarity (*prasāda*) manifests the meaning instantaneously, and because it manifests the quality of clarity residing in the aforementioned *rasa* and *bhāva*, its presence in the composition (*racanā*)— even though it is subordinate— is stated as being subject to effort through its association with *rasa*, even when there are transgressions of clarity.
Even the general [style], through its composition, manifests both the pathetic (*karuṇa*) and the erotic-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*);
that too, even when employing a medium compounding (*madhyama-samāsa*), reveals them upon abandonment [of other elements].
For example:
“O necklace of pearls, you lie upon my beloved’s breasts with a wound made by a needle’s point;
yet, with my vital organs pierced a hundred times by the arrows of Love, how is it that I do not behold her even in a dream?”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍha) "With a needle-point" refers to this speech of one separated from his beloved, addressed to the pearl necklace placed upon her breast—though out of sight, it is brought before him by his own intense emotion.
The meaning of the verse, however, is quite clear from its context.

The wise state that these [qualities] are called "having sound as their quality" (*śabdaguṇatva*) by way of metaphorical attribution (*guṇavṛtti*), just as a body is said to possess qualities such as valor; this is the implied sense. *Locanā*.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that these possess the function of words (*śabdavṛttitva*), he states the reason for this with the word "of these" (*eṣām*).

By way of figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*)—that is, by metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) according to the manner previously described—[there are] those which are known as *śleṣa*, *samādhi*, *audārya*, and *prasāda*. (VisSd 8.9)
Those qualities described by the ancients as belonging to *ojas* are included within *ojaḥ*;
for the term *aujaḥ* refers, by way of figurative usage (*bhakti*), to a specific property of word (*śabda*) or meaning (*artha*) that is denoted by the word *ojaḥ*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) She establishes the conventional usage of these [qualities] as being qualities of sound (*śabda-guṇatva*)—namely, "of these" (*eṣām*).

By means of figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*), that is, by indirect application (*paramparāvṛtti*), their status as qualities of sound is indicated indirectly through their capacity to manifest the *rasas* which are themselves the substrata of those qualities; this is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The quality of meaning (*arthaguṇatva*) should also be understood in this same way.

Thus, the three qualities that reside solely in *rasa* (taste) are, through a mediated succession, those that reside in both word and meaning. As stated by the ancients: "Cohesion (*śleṣa*), clarity (*prasāda*), evenness (*samatā*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), delicacy (*sukumāratā*),..."

"Explicitness of meaning (arthavyakti), loftiness (audārya), vigor (ojas), grace (kānti), and composure (samādhi)—among these ten qualities, the four beginning with *śleṣa* are included within *ojas*. Thus he says: 'Coalescence (*śleṣa*)', and so forth.
Regarding the manner in which they are included within *ojas*, he says: 'by way of figurative application (*bhaktyā*)'.
For those four qualities reside precisely in the phonemes that manifest the quality of *ojas* as we have described it; thus it is said by them."

And thus, through a traditional application of the term *śabda*, those [qualities] in their own system ultimately resolve into being the very substrata for the presence of the *ojaḥ* quality as we have described it.

Likewise, since it would be cumbersome to state that they are distinct from that [quality], it is more appropriate to say they are identical to it; this is precisely what he expresses with the word "figuratively" (*bhaktyā*).

The meaning is that by means of a figurative application in the form of a traditional succession, they are included within the property of *śabda* (sound/word) with respect to the specific *rasa* and *guṇa* denoted by the word *ojaḥ*.
The meaning is that these [words] are non-different from that [meaning].
In this context, *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) consists in the appearance of even many words as if they were a single word.
*Locanā*:

(Lo, Au) To the question "Why are there only three qualities? he says: "Coalescence" (śleṣa). This is by way of figurative usage (bhakti); that is, the appearance of many words as if they were a single word.
For example:

"Just as this sound, which rends the path of hearing, rises up loudly— making all the regions within the mountain caves echo by means of the continuous impact of the splashing of the lordly elephants of the water emerging [from the sea]— so too does this tide rise, white with countless conchs swaying about in abundance."

This [quality] is indeed *ojas* (vigor), because its nature consists in the density of compounds (*bandha-vaikaṭya*). Regarding this, [the author] states the definition of *śleṣa* (punning condensation) as expressed by them: "Punning condensation (*śleṣa*) is [the conjunction] of many...
[Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta)] ...In that regard, he states the definition of *śleṣa* mentioned by them: "Punning condensation (*śleṣa*) is [the conjunction] of many..."
The appearance as a single word occurs through a long compound.

Regarding the term *unmajjat*: because of the continuous forceful splashing by the lordly elephant in the water as he emerges—being uplifted by that sudden act of splashing—this sound issues forth loudly; this is likely used here in the sense of a conjecture (*sambhāvanā*).
Likewise, the tide of the ocean surges forth with water;
the meaning is that it floods the shore by the splashing of elephants.
Of what nature is the tide? It is white with countless, trembling, and moving conch shells.
What is the nature of this sound?
It pierces the path of hearing,
and it causes all the interiors of mountain caves to resound with echoes.
"This" refers to the density of compounds and the quality of words distinguished by bold strength (*ojas*).
And since that [density] resides in such words, the meaning is that it is, through a mediated succession, nothing other than the *ojaḥ* quality residing in words.
The sense is that there is complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating two properties in a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
Locanā:
This is very clear in cases such as "the sound resonates loudly" (*uccair uccarati dhvaniḥ*).
The "water-elephant" (*jalakuñjara*) is a particular aquatic creature with a face shaped like that of an elephant.
Its "impetuous impact" (*rabhasenāsphālaḥ*)— meaning the striking or agitation of the water itself— is what causes them to "swing" (*preṅkhantaḥ*) or leap about (*valgantaḥ*).
"Velā" refers to the ocean wave;
"samādhi" refers to the sequence of ascending and descending,
where "ascending" means excellence.
Avaroha (descent) is a downward progression; the sequence of these two [ascent and descent] arranged so as not to produce a sense of weariness is *vinyāsa* (arrangement).
For example: “cañcadbhuja—” and so forth.
Here, in the first three quarters, there is a progressive intensification of the bond;
however, in the fourth quarter, there is a reduction.
Yet even that [reduction] possesses vigor due to its being uttered with intense effort.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) He states the definition of the basis of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—namely, "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*).
Excellence depends upon meditative concentration; decline depends upon its absence.
Regarding "the sequence of these two":
sequence consists in the non-production of distaste through the placement [of the letters] in the previously mentioned locations;
thus he says, "it brings about distaste."
"Cañcadbhuja" and so forth—
this has been explained previously.
"The tightness of the bond"— due to the long compound, that itself constitutes excellence.
Regarding the fourth quarter:

in the verse, “O Queen, Bhīma will braid your hair,” the absence of a long compound constitutes *apakarṣa* (deficiency). Here, in the form of Draupadī’s consolation, the absence of a long compound is due to the absence of anger; because it is placed in an appropriate position, it does not produce a sense of distaste.
For this very reason, even "falling excellence" (*patatprakarṣatva*) is a quality (*guṇa*) here.
He shows that this too is included within *ojas* with the words "of this too.
Thus, the sense is that its inclusion within *ojas* occurs by virtue of the first three quarters [of the verse].
Magnificence (*udāratā*) is characterized by grandiosity (*vikaṭatva*). Grandiosity is the state of words being as if they were dancing. — *Locanā* —
(Lo, ā) "The state of being as if dancing": where words, having been turned into dancers, are experienced as if they were displayed. For example—

There, the anklets of the dancing girls, set upon their beautiful feet, produced a wonderful and melodious *jhaṇiti* sound. And here, according to that [author’s] opinion, there is *ojas* (vigorousness) through mere verbal artifice (*śabdaprauḍhokti*) alone, even without the contemplation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Vijñapriyā: The *jhaṇiti* sound of the anklets of the dancing girls, placed upon their lovely feet, was both marvelous and sweet there. And in this case, following his view, there is *ojas* by means of verbal artifice alone, even in the absence of the apprehension of *rasa*.
(vi, da) He states the characteristic of *audāryya* (magnificence): "And it is exemplified," etc.
Its state of being as if dancing is to be understood through experience alone; it cannot be described, but is to be realized in the example.
[The phrase] "by her own feet," etc., [is explained as follows].
This is a verse of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment. Short *repha*s, short *śa*s, and brevity of compounds are the manifestors of its sweetness (*mādhurya*).

Nevertheless, according to that [opponent’s] view, because the experience of the *guṇa* of *ojas* occurs even before the contemplation of such a sentiment—due merely to the knowledge of the "matured expression" (*prauḍhokti*) consisting of the words' tendency toward dancing—he says: "In this [verse], according to that view."

And thus, even here in the context of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), when such maturity (*prauḍhi*) is manifested, the sense is that the quality of vigor (*ojas*) as described by us is included within the quality of loftiness (*audārya*).
Clarity (*prasāda*) consists in a relaxation of structure mixed with vigor;
for example: [Example omitted per instructions]
"Whosoever, out of the great pride in his own arms, wields a weapon against the armies of the Pāṇḍavas... [Thus it is said].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, dha) states the definition of the quality of clarity (*prasāda*) as follows: "Clarity," etc.
The meaning is the blending of hard and soft colors.
"Whichever [color]" has been explained previously.
Here, there is brilliance (*ojasvitā*) due to the blending even of hard colors.
The capacity of the absence of compounds to manifest sweetness has been demonstrated.
Furthermore, the state of having separate words (*pṛthakpadatva*) has been accepted as *mādhurya* (sweetness) by him [Bhāmaha] himself.
*Vijñapriyā*:

[The author] says "mādhuryya... [etc. to show that the definition of *mādhurya* is the state of having separate words, and that this very thing has been accepted by us as a non-compound (*asamāsa*) which manifests *mādhurya*.
In "she releases sighs" (*śvāsān muñcati*), there is no compound.
Locanā:
(lo, i) The absence of compounding has been described by the phrase "either non-compounding or minimal compounding."
As in the passage beginning with “He releases his breath,” the manifestation of meaning is subsumed precisely by the quality known as clarity (prasāda).

The clarity of meaning (*arthavyakti*) consists in the words' immediate delivery of the sense; a clear example [is provided]. Beauty (*kānti*) and delicacy (*sukumāratā*) result from the avoidance of vulgarity and harshness. (VisSd 8.12)
The connection is that [this quality] is accepted.
And that consists in possessing a non-worldly beauty through the reversal of the placement of words found in [the speech of] plowmen and the like.
*Sukumāratā* (delicacy) is the absence of harshness.
The examples for these two are clear.
*Vijñapriyā*: "The example is clear."
The phrase beginning with "sūcimukhena" and so forth serves as an illustration of the quality of clarity (*prasāda*), as it is one among many such illustrations.
"Absence of harshness" (*apāruṣya*) means the state of not being unpleasant to hear.
These two are the examples [of these qualities].
The meaning is that these verses alone are free from these two defects.

Locanā: (lo, ī) As for beauty, it is as in my [verse]: "Her eyes are like the *khañjana* bird; her two hands rival the lotus; and her breasts attain a towering height that puts to shame the frontal globes of an elephant."
Her luster rivals the golden campaka flower; her speech vies with nectar; and the radiance of her sidelong glances is like a garland of blooming blue lotuses.
In some cases, however, even a fault is equanimity, whose nature is the non-differentiation of the path;
otherwise, it falls within the aforementioned qualities as appropriate.
The non-deviation from the path (*mārgābheda*) consists in the completion of a composition that has been commenced by means of either a smooth or a rugged path, using that very same path.
And this is sometimes a fault; for instance:
“Though this lion cub bears a body with limbs not yet fully developed and a belly that has not grown large enough for its paws, why should he be measured merely by the size of his palms?
For, out of wrath at the drying up of the flood of ichor from hundreds of rutting, uncontrollable scent-elephants, the fire of the world’s end (kalpāgni) is rendered small before him.”
In this case, when the intended meaning is *uddhata* (elevated), the abandonment of a delicate composition (*sukumārabandha*) is indeed a merit (*guṇa*).
In instances other than these, it falls within the category of *mādhurya* (sweetness) and so forth.
For example: "latākuñjaṃ guñjan—" and so on.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
pha) "In some cases" means that equanimity,
which demonstrates the non-differentiation of the path, is in some instances a fault.
Regarding the term "otherwise" (*anyathā*):
in such a case, the meaning is that there is an equilibrium of the qualities of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and vigor (*ojas*), or one of those two qualities.
He explains this with the words "by means of the smooth [sound]" (*masṛṇena*).

Regarding the phrase "avyūḍhāṅgam" (with undeveloped limbs): the lion, the lord of beasts, bears that body with its limbs undeveloped—that is, with parts not yet matured—and lacking fullness through the expansion of its paws and belly; thus, due to its smallness, it can fit within the hollow of a hand.

What is gained by this much? From this visible [act]—by the drying up of the oceans of the fierce ichor of a hundred elephants (*sindhura*) with their hundreds of tusks and their overflowing seas of rut—the fire at the end of an aeon (*kalpāgni*) is rendered insignificant once again.
"Not of such a kind" means when the subject matter (*vācya*) is not boastful.

A defect (*doṣa*), however, should be understood as being of the nature of the opposite of these [excellences]. Since the absence of these constitutes a defect, the excellences residing in the meaning (*arthagā guṇāḥ*)—namely, vigor (*ojas*), clarity (*prasāda*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), delicacy (*saukumārya*), and loftiness (*udāratā*)—are accepted [as such]. (VisSd 8.14)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ba) Now, he states the reason for not accepting even the ten qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇa*) mentioned by others, despite their having distinct characteristics from those names already mentioned: "Ojas, Prasāda," and so forth.
The meaning is that the five qualities of meaning, beginning with *ojas* and ending with *udāra*, are already accepted [as such] precisely because their absence constitutes a defect (*doṣa*).
And thus, the meaning is that these five qualities are indeed the absence of defects:
*ojas* consists in being full of intentionality,
and *prasāda* is the clarity of the meaning.

Sweetness (*mādhurya*), variety of expression (*ukti-vicitrya*), delicacy (*saukumārya*), absence of harshness (*apāruṣya*), and loftiness (*udāratā*)— which is the same as non-vulgarity (*agrāmyatva*): the acceptance of these five qualities of meaning (*artha-guṇa*) occurs precisely through the exclusion, respectively, of those meanings that are underdeveloped (*apuṣṭārtha*), redundant (*adhikapada*), unrefined (*anavīkṛta*), inauspicious (*amaṅgalarūpa*), indecorous (*aślīla*), and vulgar (*grāmya*).
The examples are clear.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, bha) states the definitions of the five qualities beginning with *ojas*: "Regarding *ojas*... and so forth.
Intentionality (*sābhiprāyatva*) consists in being an adjective intended to nourish the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
This is accepted as the absence of the fault of "lack of significance" (*apuṣṭārthatva*).
Clarity of meaning (*arthavaimalya*) is the non-defilement by superfluous words (*adhikapada*).

And that [quality] is a variety of expression (*ukti-vaicitrya*) by virtue of being the absence of the fault of pleonasm (*adhika-pada-tva*); it is the statement of a meaning that must be presented many times in a different manner, and that [variety of expression] is the absence of the fault of lack of novelty (*anavīkṛtatva*). Non-roughness (*apāruṣya*) is the absence of roughness consisting of inauspiciousness.
And that [absence of vulgarity] consists in being distinct from meanings that convey coarseness or lack of refinement, by virtue of the absence of the defects of inauspiciousness and indecorum;
and the meaning is that this is accepted as the very absence of the defect of vulgarity.

"Clear" (spaṣṭāni) means that these verses are indeed free from the aforementioned five defects. Furthermore, clarity (*arthavyakti*) arises through the ornament of *svabhāvokti* (natural description), as well as through the suggestion of aesthetic flavor (*rasadhvani*) and the suggested meaning as a subordinate element (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*); this is what is called "loveliness" (*kānti*). (VisSd 8.15)
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ma) "The chamber of love is empty," and so forth— this is *rasadhvani*, where rasa is the subordinate suggested meaning (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).
"This is that [act] of lifting the tongue," and so forth, refers to another subordinate element (*aṅga*).
It is connected with the word "accepted" (*aṅgīkṛta*).
*Arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning) is the vividness of the essential nature of the subject matter (*vastu-svabhāva*).
Locanā:

(lo, u) Regarding the phrase "prodyaddurdhara" and so forth, it refers to the clarity of meaning (*arthavyakti*). For example: "Having struck with his tail and repeatedly tearing at the surface of the earth with his forefeet, then suddenly crouching down upon himself and leaping swiftly into the sky with great force..."
With a terrible, hissing roar resounding in every direction, this hyena, possessed by rage and with eyes red and swollen, has entered every forest, warding off all living creatures.
Luster is the quality of brilliance;
the examples are clear. Alliteration is merely a form of variety and is not a fault; evenness is supreme.
Vijñapriyā:

"Merely a variety"—that is to say, since variety is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and because it is thus pervaded by the general definition of an ornament, this is indeed an ornament and not a quality (*guṇa*); such is the meaning. [The term] "evenness" (*samatā*)...
Equanimity (*samatā*) is the supreme fault; the meaning is that it is merely the absence of faults.
*Śleṣa* (cohesion) consists of the arrangement of form through the connection of logical justification, characterized by sequence, curvature, lack of abruptness, and appropriateness.
Among these, sequence (*krama*) is the continuity of actions.
Cleverness of action is *kauṭilya* (artfulness);

the absence of description of what is not well-known is *anulvaṇatva* (lack of vulgarity); and the arrangement of supporting arguments is *upapatti* (justification). The conjunction—that is, the combination—of these is the very form of the composition; such a *śleṣa* (conjunction) is merely a matter of aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*).
The meaning is that it lacks the excellence of being assisted by a rasa that is not shared with anything else.
Regarding this, [the author] states the definition of *śleṣa* (punning condensation): "The sequence of *śleṣa*," and so forth.
He explains *krama* and the others: "sequence is performed"—the meaning is an abundance of expectant actions.

He analyzes the *bahuvrīhi* compound beginning with "sequence and curvature" (*kramakauṭilya*) as "that which has that very thing as its form. The meaning is "that very [sequence] is their conjunction (*yoga*)."
In the phrase "of that nature" (*tadrūpa*), the word *rūpa* (nature) is an explanation of the referent of the word *ātman* (self).
Regarding the term "not other" (*ananya*):
sweetness and so forth are either included within that [nature] or are distinct qualities; for example, they are the cause of an excellence in the assistance provided to a distinct flavor (*rasa*).
The meaning is that because of the absence of suchness (tathātva), there is no status as a *guṇa* (poetic quality).
For example:
"Having seen her beloved standing in a solitary place," and so forth.
In this context, the actions are seeing and so forth;
the crookedness consists in the form of supporting both [sides].
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, la) *Dṛṣṭvaika*— having seen that pair, the beloved and her lover, seated together on a single seat, the clever hero approaches from behind; under the pretext of continuing their play, he covers the eyes of one with his own two hands, and with his neck slightly bent, his hair standing on end, he kisses the other with great affection.
What is the other [type]?
It is one whose cheeks shine with an inner smile from a heart overflowing with love, and who possesses horripilation;
this is the "supporting both"—namely, the anger of the one whose eyes were covered.

Both the pleasure of being kissed and [the desire for] kissing are supported by walking behind her and closing her eyes; this support takes the form of "support" (samarthana) through the artful gestures and the guile of physical form.
In this context, the lack of vulgarity consists in the worldly convention regarding the act itself, as they remained seated on the same seat.
The phrases "having approached from behind," "having covered the eyes," and "with the neck slightly bent" are the supporting elements; their conjunction constitutes [the figure].

And because of the preoccupation with grasping the justification of the expressed meaning, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth remain largely obscured; thus, this lack of immediate connection is not a defect.
Furthermore, *samatā* (evenness) is the absence of contradiction in the meaning through the non-inversion of the intended roots and suffixes.
And that [defect] consists precisely in the absence of the proper arrangement of the sequence;
the example is clear.
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding "worldly convention" (*lokavyavahāra*): this is because other people in the world also act in this manner.

Regarding "justifying factors" (*upapādakāni*): the meaning is that they serve to justify the kissing performed by the co-wife while she is invisible. He demonstrates the absence of its being a poetic quality (*guṇa*) with the words "and by this."

The meaning is that the aesthetic relish (*rasāsvāda*) for those perceivers who understand [the intended sense] through kissing, subsequent approach, and so forth—which are the means of accomplishing the apprehension [of the object]—is, due to the distraction of the rogue, as if mediated (*vyavahita*); the implication is that it is somewhat delayed.
Regarding "already commenced" (*prakrānta*): the meaning is the similarity between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) which have already been introduced or are being introduced.

"Clearly" means that it is precisely a verse free from the fault of breaking the established sequence; it does not mean that the *samādhi* (resolution) possesses the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇa*).

And meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has two kinds of objective referents (*artha*): that which is not born from another’s reflection (*ayoni*), and that which is born from another’s reflection (*anyonyacchāyāyoni*).
Among these, the referent that is not born from another’s reflection is as follows:
"The orange fruit vies with the chin of a drunken Hun who has just been shaven."

Another example of arising from a shadow is as follows: “Deceived many times by the reflections of her own eyes in the water, a certain flower-gatherer even hesitates to place her hand upon a blue lotus.”

In this instance, the well-known similarity between the blue lotus and the eyes is expressed through a specific poetic charm (*vicchitti*). Because this [similarity] does not impart any extraordinary beauty, it possesses no status as a poetic quality (*guṇa*); rather, its function is merely to bring about the formal body of the poem.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, śa) "Ayoni" refers to a meaning not described by others;
"anyacchāyāyoni" refers to that which follows a meaning described by others; and "sadyas" means immediate.
The Hūṇa is a Yavana from a specific western region,
and he is copper-colored; moreover, due to his state of intoxication, he is exceedingly copper-red.
The *nāraṅgaka* is the orange fruit, slightly copper-colored;
this meaning has not been described by others.
Regarding the phrase "her own eyes": a certain flower-gatherer, the wife of a gardener, mistook the reflection of her own eyes in the water for blue lotuses.
The meaning is that, having been incited toward grasping it, and being thus deceived by not obtaining it, she deliberates whether or not it is possible to apply her hand even to a real blue lotus;
this is the shadow of another described meaning.
"And of this"—the sense is that there is no contribution to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) due to a confusion regarding the body.
*Locanā*:
(Lo, Ū) "Unprecedented" (*ayoni*) means a meaning not seen by previous poets.
This [prolixity] serves solely to sustain the body of the poem, because the body of the poem cannot be sustained except through these two modes.
For instance, when a single object such as "the moon" ought to be mentioned, there is the use of a sentence such as "the light arising from the eye of Atri.
— *Locanā* —
(Lo, Ṛ) "Vākyavacana" (expression by means of a sentence) refers to the designation of a collection of words.

For instance, when the meaning of a sentence such as "a woman whose limbs are delicate and who possesses a body both cool in summer and warm in winter" is to be expressed, there is the use of the single-word expression "varavarṇinī" (a woman of excellent complexion).
— *Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ṣa) Another [quality] is *prauḍhi* (boldness), which others have called the quality of *ojas* (vigour). Regarding that, four kinds of *prauḍhi* have been stated by others: the composition of a sentence regarding the meaning of a word, the expression of a word regarding the meaning of a sentence, the use of prefixes (*prādi*), and the use of expansion (*vyāsa*) and contraction (*samāsa*).

To show that it is not appropriate to claim its status as a quality (*guṇatva*), he demonstrates its expression as a word-meaning (*padārtha*) or as a sentence-structure (*vākyaracanā*) by saying: "In some cases, 'the moon'...
He shows the designation of a word for the meaning of a sentence by saying: "In some cases, 'the heat'... [As it is said:
"It may be hot during the cold season, and pleasantly cool during the summer."
"Endowed with the beauty of every limb, she is remembered as a woman of excellent complexion (*varavarṇinī*).
Thus [the author] demonstrates the definition of *varavarṇinī*.
*Vyāsa* (expansion) is of the nature wherein a single sentence-meaning is expressed through multiple sentences by the introduction of some particular qualification in each case.
Furthermore, there is the type of *samāsa* (condensation) where that which is expounded by many sentences is expressed by a single sentence; as stated in the *Locanā*:

(Lo, ṛ) "The presentation of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthanyāsa*) is, for example: 'This manifold experience of the intermingling of pleasure and pain—whether it be pleasure or pain—arises and indeed comes to pass for you.'"
"Therefore, one becomes superior, experiencing neither suffering nor pleasure.
This is its summary, as follows: "Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped:
do not practice toward others those things which are disagreeable to oneself. Thus [it is said].
It is not appropriate for such things as these, mentioned by others, to be considered *guṇas* (poetic excellences).
*Locanā*:
(Lo, Ḷ) "Not being a *guṇa*"—the sense is that this is because they lack the quality of assisting the *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) in a manner unique to themselves.
Thus [ends the section].
Thus concludes the eighth chapter, titled "The Definition of Qualities" (*guṇanirūpaṇa*), in the *Sāhityadarpaṇalocana*.
Rather, it is that which brings about mere aesthetic charm (*vaicitryamātrāvahatva*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, sa) "In some cases, of one"—that is, due to a distinction, meaning due to a specific interruption, [it is] by means of speaking in fragmentary sentences.

For example, when it ought to be stated in a single sentence that "this man is not learned," one speaks of his ignorance of all the sciences through fragmentary sentences such as "he does not know grammar" or "he does not know logic," and so forth.
He shows the summary: "in some cases, as shown" (*kvacidūhyeti*).

This refers to the reversal of the previously shown expansion—that is, the condensation of that which has many points to be explained or is expressed through many sentences—by means of phrases such as "and so forth" (*evamādīnām*).
The meaning is: of the four kinds of *prauḍhi* (dignified elaboration) described by others as being the quality of *ojas* (vigorousness).
The meaning is that since it is merely a variety [of the same thing], this is indeed nothing other than a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
Thus ends the commentary on the eighth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Qualities" (*guṇavivecana*), in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Maheśvara Nyāyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya.
Therefore, there are no separate qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇas*). VisSd 8.16.
In the manner thus described,
the qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇa*), such as *ojas* and the rest, have been explained.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Qualities," in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
